author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The Japanese yen’s advance toward a seven-month high is putting renewed pressure on a long-running strategy used across global markets: the yen carry trade.

In a carry trade, investors borrow in a currency with relatively low interest rates and invest the proceeds in higher-yielding currencies or assets. The approach benefited from Japan’s years of very easy monetary policy, especially when U.S. rates rose sharply in 2022 and 2023.

That advantage can shrink when the yen strengthens or Japanese borrowing costs rise. Markets now expect the Bank of Japan may tighten policy, raising the risk that investors must unwind leveraged positions. Reuters reported yen-based cross-border borrowing reached a record 360 trillion yen in March, though the full size of carry trades is difficult to measure.

The current adjustment appears more anticipated than the abrupt 2024 unwind, but currency and rate moves can still transmit volatility across stocks, bonds and emerging markets. The figures describe reported positioning and delayed market conditions, not a live quote or investment recommendation.
dek: Expectations for Bank of Japan tightening are narrowing the advantage of borrowing cheaply in yen to buy higher-yielding assets.
headline: Stronger yen puts carry trade under renewed pressure
